newsitem.title: UK: Oil price steady as U.S. troops arrive in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Oil price steady as U.S. troops arrive in Gulf.

text.p: World oil prices on Tuesday stemmed a sharp decline from last week's five-year highs as the United States moved more troops and weaponry into the oil-rich Gulf region to face Iraq.
November futures for international benchmark Brent crude ended up 13 cents at $21.73 a barrel.

Washington said two Patriot anti-missile batteries and U.S. soldiers to operate them had arrived in Saudi Arabia and President Bill Clinton said he had ordered the deployment of extra troops to Kuwait on Monday night.
But the foreign ministers of France and Saudi Arabia urged restraint in the region. The two countries were key members of the U.S.-led coalition that drove Iraq out of Kuwait in 1991.
Oil prices rose sharply after Iraqi troops intervened in Kurdish factional fighting two weeks ago, prompting the United Nations to postpone implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food plan.
A subsequent buildup of U.S. military might in the Gulf, which supplies 40 percent of world oil output, raised fears of supply disruptions and took prices to a five-year high last Thursday.

Prices tumbled on Monday, initially on perceptions of an easing of tension in the Gulf and later on an unfounded report that the United States had asked Saudi Arabia to raise production to compensate for the delay in Iraqi oil exports.

Gulf sources and the State Department denied any such request was made to any member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). The sources said Saudi Arabia would adhere to its 8.0 million barrels per day (bpd) OPEC quota.
OPEC meets in November to discuss a new overall ceiling, currently set at 25.033 million bpd, which makes provision for the increased Iraqi oil which had been expected in September.
"There have been no discussion at all on this matter. It is too early to say what we will do in November," a Gulf source familiar with Saudi policy said.

Iraqi oil has been under a U.N. embargo since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990. A deal reached with the United Nations on May 20 allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicines but has now been postponed indefinitely.

Analysts say that with demand for crude expected to pick up in October ahead of the northern hemisphere winter, the estimated 700,000 bpd of Iraqi oil would have been absorbed by the market, particularly with heating oil stocks very low.
Saudi Arabia has 2.0 million bpd of spare capacity but traders said any formal increase in OPEC's ceiling was likely to lead to a fall in prices.

"If OPEC were smart, they would just continue to quietly feed the market extra barrels rather than make a big announcement by raising the ceiling," said Bo Van Wijk, vice president of energy risk management at Swiss bank UBS.
